items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Different metals have different arrangements of ions in the lattice. Do not worry too much about this when drawing a diagram of a metal. As long as you draw the ions in a regular arrangement that will be fine.

items.label: text
items.text: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic forces of attraction between each positive ion and the delocalised electrons. This holds the structure together.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: When they come to write the symbol for a metal such as sodium in equations, students who know about metallic bonding sometimes worry whether they should write it as Na or Na*. You write it as atoms, as Na. Thinking about the structure as a whole, the number of electrons exactly balances the number of positive charges. The metal as a whole carries no charge.

items.label: section_header
items.text: METALS CONDUCT ELECTRICITY

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: In Chapter 7 we discussed ionic compounds and how they conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution because the ions are free to move. lonic substances do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are not free to move. Metals conduct electricity when solid or molten because the delocalised electrons are free to move. It is important not to confuse this:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 9.4 The electrostatic attraction between positively charged ions and negatively charged electrons holds the metallic structure together.

items.label: text
items.text: Metals have giant structures. There are no individual molecules and all the positive ions in the lattice attract all the delocalised electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: The ion formed by the metal depends on the number of electrons the original atom has in its outer shell. Thus all the elements in Group 1 form 1+ ions and all the elements in Group 2 form 2+ ions.

items.label: section_header
items.text: PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF METALS

items.label: text
items.text: Most metals are hard and have high melting points. This suggests that the electrostatic forces of attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons are strong.

items.label: text
items.text: In the case of sodium, only one electron per atom is delocalised, leaving ions with only one positive charge on them. The bonding in sodium is quite weak, as metals go, which is why sodium is fairly soft, with a low melting point for a metal. Magnesium has two outer electrons, both of which are delocalised into the 'sea', leaving behind ions that carry a charge of 2+. There is a much stronger electrostatic attraction between the 2+ ions and the delocalised electrons. This means that the bonding is stronger in magnesium and the melting point is higher.

items.label: text
items.text: Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons are free to move throughout the structure. Imagine what happens if a piece of metal is attached to an electrical power source.

items.label: list_item
items.text: ionic substances: ions move

items.label: list_item
items.text: metals: electrons move

items.label: section_header
items.text: METALS ARE MALLEABLE

items.label: text
items.text: electrons attracted to this end by the positive terminal of the power source and then flow away along the wire more electrons flow along the wire from the negative terminal of the power source to replace those moving away in the metal

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 9.5 How metals conduct electricity.

items.label: text
items.text: Metals can be hammered into different shapes; this is what the word malleable means. When we apply a force to a piece of metal the layers of positive ions slide over each other. This does not affect the bonding in the structure; the positive ions are still attracted to the delocalised electrons.
